# Cucumber, BDD and Gherkin, Warranting Agent-Built Software Distillation

**Source:** Cucumber. *Cucumber documentation: Behaviour-Driven Development and the Gherkin reference* (the BDD and Gherkin sections), repository https://github.com/cucumber/website at commit 2014c06d69db5927f6a0106b3a4ea08d7acec885 (2026-10-08). MIT licence; Copyright 2014 Aslak Hellesøy and contributors. Scope: open. Adaptation notice: this distillation paraphrases and quotes the source; changes were made.

**Coverage: PARTIAL, operator-approved 2026-10-14.** The deep reference covers the BDD and Gherkin sections of the Cucumber documentation, every page of each, read in full. The rest of the site (installation, language-specific guides, the step-definitions and API pages, the anti-patterns guide, the blog) is not taken, so nothing here describes it.

**Applicability gate (Pass G.0): clear yes.** (1) The source answers a practitioner question this axis asks first: is "correct" for this change written down somewhere a machine can check, or only in the agent's summary? Its whole method is concrete examples, agreed with the business, written in a form both people and machines read, and automated as tests before the code. (2) Its concepts land naturally in Phase 1 and Phase 3, and support four more. (3) Its contrarian positions (automating after the code is "not BDD"; running Cucumber is no proof of doing BDD; discovery by one person is "not BDD") speak to the axis's first reflex, an assertion taken as evidence.

**Phase mapping.** Primary: Phase 1, Specifying the change (discovery, Example Mapping, concrete examples, behaviour not implementation, story size) and Phase 3, Locking the tests (examples automated before the code, a test that fails first, outcomes checked on observable output, scenario versus step definition). Supporting: Phase 4, Building in the sandbox (one example at a time; no step definitions nobody's scenario uses); Phase 5, Gating deterministically (a scenario that passes before the code exists; scenarios Cucumber silently ignores); Phase 6, Reviewing independently (scenarios a non-programmer can read; the product owner's review of what a pair wrote); Phase 7, Warranting the change (living documentation as the record of what the system does; a green Cucumber run is not proof the behaviour was agreed). One row: Phase 8, Releasing and operating (documentation checked against the system on every run, so docs and code cannot drift apart unseen). No rows: Phase 2, Triaging risk. The source sorts no change by what it touches or what it can break.

**Transfer caveat.** The source is product documentation for human teams. It says nothing about coding agents, and it reports no studies or measurements: its recommendations, rules of thumb and myths are the documentation's practitioner assertions, marked `[AP]` or `[AR]`, not demonstrated findings. Where this distillation carries a recommendation into an agent harness (an agent as the developer, a scenario file as the locked specification), the step is this distillation's inference and says so.

## Warranting Agent-Built Software Relevance

A builder warranting agent-built software needs "correct" written down before the agent starts, in a form that a person can agree to and a machine can run. This source supplies one worked method for that. Concrete examples of the behaviour are discovered in a short conversation between the people who know the domain and the people who build and test; they are formulated in Gherkin, "a medium that can be read by both humans and computers" [V]; then each is automated as a test that fails before the code exists, and the code is built until it passes (Source: Cucumber, BDD and Gherkin docs, docs/bdd/index.md, "Three practices"; "Formulation: What it _should_ do"; "Automation: What it _actually does_") [AP]. For the warranty, that turns acceptance criteria from prose the agent interprets into checks the agent did not get to define alone, and it gives the accountable builder something to read instead of the diff: the scenarios, written in the client's language.

The source also draws lines a gate can enforce. Scenarios describe behaviour, not implementation, so a scenario should not need to change when only the implementation does (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Describe behaviour") [AR]. Outcomes are checked on what comes out of the system, not on what sits inside it (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Then") [AP]. Behaviour lives in the feature file; implementation lives in the step definitions (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "When") [AP]. And the documentation is blunt that the tool is not the practice: "Just because you're using Cucumber, doesn't mean you're doing BDD." [V] (docs/bdd/myths.md, "Myth: Using Cucumber means you're doing BDD"). A green Cucumber run shows the code meets the scenarios; whether those scenarios capture what the client needs depends on how they were discovered and who agreed them. These are the source's practitioner assertions; none is measured.

## Key Concepts for Warranting Agent-Built Software

1. <!-- concept: discovery-formulation-automation --> **Three practices, in order.** Discovery (talk about concrete examples of a small change), Formulation (document them so they can be automated, and check for agreement), Automation (implement each example starting from an automated test) (Source: Cucumber, BDD and Gherkin docs, docs/bdd/index.md, "Three practices") [AR]. The order is the point: "Unless you've already done effective discovery work, trying to formulate scenarios is a waste of time." [V] (docs/bdd/myths.md, "Myth: You can pick and choose the practices in any order"). For the harness, an agent handed a story with no discovery behind it is being asked to formulate, or to automate, without the step the source puts first.

2. <!-- concept: executable-specification --> **Executable specification.** An example is specification, documentation and test at once, and the examples together are an executable specification of the system (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Example") [AP]. The Given/When/Then template "was developed to capture a story's acceptance criteria in an executable form" [V] (docs/bdd/history.md, "Early tools supporting BDD"). This is the source's answer to "is correct written down where a machine can check it?"

3. <!-- concept: discovery-workshop --> **Discovery workshop and the Three Amigos.** A short conversation, "3-6 people" [V] including at least a product owner (scope), a developer (how to build it) and a tester (edge cases), held as late as possible before development, for "about 25-30 minutes per story" [V] (docs/bdd/discovery-workshop.md, "Who should attend?"; "How long does a discovery workshop take?"). Each role sees the product from a different perspective, so all of them should discover examples together [AR] (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "The Three Amigos"). Needing longer suggests the story is too big, or that specifics are missing and the story should be set aside for research [AP].

4. <!-- concept: example-mapping --> **Example Mapping, with questions held on red cards.** Story on a yellow card, each rule (acceptance criterion) on a blue card, concrete examples on green cards under their rule, and questions that cannot be answered in the session on red cards, so the conversation moves on (docs/bdd/example-mapping.md, "How it works") [AP]. Discussion also surfaces new stories, sliced off and deferred out of scope [AP]. For the harness, a red card is a written record of what nobody yet knows, which is what an agent would otherwise decide unseen (this distillation's inference).

5. <!-- concept: behaviour-not-implementation --> **Behaviour, not implementation.** "Your scenarios should describe the intended behaviour of the system, not the implementation." [V] The test for each clause is "Will this wording need to change if the implementation does?" [V] (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Describe behaviour"). A declarative scenario keeps its intent when the implementation changes; imperative, UI-procedural steps "often require more work to maintain" [V], though the page grants they suit some contexts (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Consider a more declarative style").

6. <!-- concept: concrete-examples --> **Concrete, technology-free examples.** Good examples name people and places, exact dates and amounts, and "don't mention technical details" [V] (docs/bdd/examples.md, "Examples"). The "Imagine it's 1922" admonition asks for examples that assume no technology or user interface, with "Implementation details should be hidden in the step definitions." [V] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "When").

7. <!-- concept: automate-before-the-code --> **Automate before the code, watch it fail.** Each example is connected to the system as a test that fails because the behaviour is not implemented yet; the code is then developed until it passes (docs/bdd/index.md, "Automation: What it _actually does_") [AP]. Automating scenarios after the code is written is "a perfectly reasonable way to do test automation, but it's not BDD." [V] (docs/bdd/myths.md, "Myth: You can automate scenarios after the code is implemented").

8. <!-- concept: observable-outcomes --> **Outcomes on observable output.** A `Then` step's definition asserts the actual outcome against the expected one, and the outcome should be something that comes out of the system (a report, user interface or message) [AP] "and not a behaviour deeply buried inside the system (like a record in a database)" [V]. On checking the database, "resist that temptation!" [V], since database changes are usually not observable for the user (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Then").

9. <!-- concept: scenario-versus-step-definition --> **Scenario versus step definition.** The feature file states behaviour in the domain's language; the step definitions are "the glue to the actual code" [V] and hold the implementation details, the exact values and the mechanics of interaction (docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx, "Avoid duplication"; docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Consider a more declarative style") [AP]. In a declarative scenario, what a `Then` step actually checks is decided in its step definition (this distillation's reading of the source's subscription example).

10. <!-- concept: living-documentation --> **Living documentation as shared understanding.** Over time the documented examples become an asset for changing the system confidently: "The code reflects the documentation, and the documentation reflects the team's shared understanding of the problem domain." [V] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Three practices"). The automated examples help the team understand what the system currently does and change it without unintentionally breaking anything [AP] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Automation: What it _actually does_").

11. <!-- concept: collaborative-discovery --> **Discovery is a conversation, not a solo task.** Teams that leave identifying examples and formulating scenarios to a single individual are "not BDD" [V]; discovery must bring together "representatives of the different specialists who all need to share understanding about what will be built" [V] (docs/bdd/myths.md, "Myth: Discovery doesn't need a conversation"). Later, a developer and a tester can pair on writing Gherkin, provided the product owner actively reviews their output (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Writing Gherkin") [AP].

12. <!-- concept: small-scenarios --> **Small, single-purpose scenarios and stories.** A scenario that cannot be described in one sentence is "probably trying to cover too much" [V] and should be split (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Scenarios"); "we recommend 3-5 steps per example" [V] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Example"); and a story that needs more than a short workshop is probably too large (docs/bdd/discovery-workshop.md) [AP]. Rules of thumb, not measured thresholds.

## Questions to Ask During Warranting Agent-Built Software

### Phase 1: Specifying the change

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Know whether "correct" is checkable | Is each acceptance criterion a rule with at least one concrete example under it (names, dates, amounts), or is it prose the agent will interpret? | docs/bdd/example-mapping.md, "How it works"; docs/bdd/examples.md |
| Know who agreed the examples | Did someone who owns the scope, someone who will build it and someone hunting edge cases discuss these examples together, or did one person (or one agent) write them alone? | docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "The Three Amigos"; docs/bdd/myths.md |
| Find what the agent would decide unseen | Which questions came up that nobody could answer, and are they written down as open (red cards) rather than left for the agent to settle? | docs/bdd/example-mapping.md, "How it works" |
| Know who the change is for | Do the `In order to`, `As a` and `I want` lines say why, for whom and what, in the client's terms? | docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Writing features" |
| Keep the spec free of implementation | Would any scenario's wording need to change if the implementation did? If so, which steps are procedure rather than behaviour? | docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Describe behaviour" |
| Size the change | Could the story's examples be agreed in about half an hour, and can each scenario be described in one sentence? If not, what can be split off or deferred? | docs/bdd/discovery-workshop.md; docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Scenarios" |
| State what must stay true | Which existing scenarios describe behaviour this change must not alter, and are they in the suite the change has to pass? | docs/bdd/index.md, "Automation: What it _actually does_"; docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md |

### Phase 3: Locking the tests

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Know the tests came before the code | Was each scenario automated and seen failing before the implementation existed, or written after the code to describe what it does? | docs/bdd/index.md, "Automation: What it _actually does_"; docs/bdd/myths.md |
| Tell a spec change from an implementation change | Did this change edit a feature file (the agreed behaviour) or only step definitions (the glue)? If a scenario changed, who agreed the new wording? | docs/bdd/index.md, "Three practices"; docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx |
| Check what the `Then` steps assert | Does each `Then` step definition assert on something that comes out of the system (a report, a screen, a message), or on a database row or the agent's own summary? | docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Then" |
| Check the step definitions carry the values | In declarative scenarios, do the step definitions pin the exact values the behaviour depends on, or do they pass whatever the system returns? | docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Consider a more declarative style" |
| Check one phrasing per meaning | Is the same thing said the same way in every scenario, so one step definition backs it? | docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Scenarios"; docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Steps" |

### Phase 4: Building in the sandbox

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Read an agent's "done" | Did the agent take one example at a time, see it fail, implement it and see it pass, or report all scenarios green at the end? | docs/bdd/index.md, "Three practices"; "Automation: What it _actually does_" |
| Catch speculative code | Did the agent write step definitions for steps no scenario uses? | docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx, "Writing step definitions" |
| Catch clutter | Did the agent add near-duplicate steps where one parameterised step with a helper method would do? | docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx, "Avoid duplication" |

### Phase 5: Gating deterministically

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Know the scenario tests the new behaviour | Did any new scenario pass on its first run, before the code it describes existed? | docs/bdd/index.md, "Automation: What it _actually does_" |
| Know every scenario ran | Does the run record show as many scenarios executed as the feature files contain, given that a misplaced colon after a keyword makes Cucumber ignore tests? | docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Reference" |

### Phase 6: Reviewing independently

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Review without reading every line | Has someone who speaks for the client read the scenarios (written for people and machines both) and confirmed they say what the client needs? | docs/bdd/index.md, "Formulation: What it _should_ do"; docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Writing Gherkin" |
| Bring the missing perspective | Has anyone asked the tester's question, how will this break, and which stories the features have not accounted for? | docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "The Three Amigos" |
| Check the scenarios read as behaviour | Could a non-programmer follow each scenario, or does it walk through fields, buttons and URLs? | docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md; docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Writing features" |

### Phase 7: Warranting the change

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Class the evidence | Does the pack cite a green Cucumber run as proof the behaviour is what the client wanted, without saying who discovered and agreed the scenarios? | docs/bdd/myths.md |
| Know the system can be explained | Do the feature files describe what this part does, in the client's language, well enough that someone could explain it without the agent session? | docs/bdd/index.md, "Three practices" |
| Know what was left open | Are any red-card questions from discovery still unanswered, and does the pack say so? | docs/bdd/example-mapping.md, "How it works" |

### Phase 8: Releasing and operating

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Catch drift between docs and code | Is the description of the system's behaviour automatically checked against the system, or is it prose that can fall out of date unseen? | docs/bdd/index.md, "What is BDD?"; "Three practices" |

## What to Look For

| Signal | Diagnosis | Follow-up |
|---|---|---|
| Acceptance criteria say "handles errors correctly" with no examples beneath them | Rules without examples; the source makes concrete examples the means of agreeing what to build (docs/bdd/index.md, "What is BDD?") [AP] | Run a short Example Mapping session: one blue card per rule, concrete green examples under each, red cards for what nobody can answer |
| The scenarios were written by the agent from the story, and nobody on the business side has read them | Discovery and formulation by one party; "That's not BDD." (docs/bdd/myths.md) [V] | Have the person who owns scope review and agree the wording before the scenarios are locked |
| Steps say "click", "fill in the field", "visit /login" | Procedural reference, not behaviour; the wording will change when the implementation does (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md) [AR] | Ask the source's question of each clause and rewrite declaratively, moving mechanics into step definitions |
| A `Then` step definition queries the database | Outcome checked inside the system rather than on observable output (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Then") [AP] | Assert on what the user or the external system sees (a report, a message, a screen) |
| A diff edits both the feature file and the code | The agreed behaviour and the implementation changed together; the scenario may have been moved to fit the code | Split the edits; route any feature-file change back to whoever agreed the scenario |
| New scenarios were all green on their first run | No evidence the scenarios test the new behaviour; the source's automation step starts with a test that fails because the behaviour is missing (docs/bdd/index.md) [AP] | Ask for the run that showed each scenario failing before the implementation |
| The run reports fewer scenarios than the feature files hold | Scenarios silently ignored, for example after a colon added to a keyword that should not have one (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Reference") [V] | Make the gate compare scenarios executed with scenarios written |
| Step definitions exist for steps no scenario uses | Speculative code; unused step definitions may become cruft to clean up later (docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx) [AP] | Remove them; implement only what the scenarios need |
| One feature carries dozens of scenarios, or scenarios run past five steps | The feature or example covers too much and loses its value as specification (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Example"; docs/bdd/who-does-what.md) [AP] | Split the feature or the scenario; collapse value variations into a `Scenario Outline` |
| The same idea is phrased two ways ("I am logged in", "I have logged in to the site") | Inconsistent domain language; "Cucumber features are best served by consistency." (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md) [V] | Pick one phrasing and use it everywhere |

## When to Use This Reference

- Reach for it in Phase 1 when a change's acceptance criteria are prose and the question is how to make them checkable with the client before the agent starts. It is the corpus's worked method for agreeing concrete examples and writing them as executable specification.
- Reach for it in Phase 3 when deciding what in the test suite is the locked specification (the scenarios) and what is implementation that may change (the step definitions), and what a `Then` step should assert on.
- Reach for it when the evidence offered is "the Cucumber suite is green" and the question is what that shows and what it does not.
- Reach for it when the accountable builder cannot read the diff and needs a readable statement of what the change does.
- Reach for another source when the question is how strong a test suite is against wrong implementations (`egashira-testsuitebench-2026`), how agent code fares against tests it did not write (`jimenez-swe-bench`), how to plan unit, integration and non-functional tests (`microsoft-code-with-engineering-playbook`, `uk-duck-book-qa-of-code`), or what a change touches and which security gates that makes mandatory (the standards and threat lists). This source has no measurements, sorts no risk and stops before release.

## Worked Example

*Scenario (operator-authored).* A two-person studio is adding a cancellation rule to a client's booking site with a coding agent. The story's acceptance criterion reads "refunds are handled correctly". The builder's instinct is to hand the story to the agent and review the result.

*Applying the source.* The builder treats the prose criterion as a gap in Phase 1. The source's method starts with a conversation, not a document: concrete examples "that illustrate how we want the system to behave" [V] (docs/bdd/index.md, "What is BDD?"), discovered with the people who know the domain. The builder runs a half-hour Example Mapping session with the client's operations lead. Two blue rule cards emerge: cancellations more than 24 hours before the booking get a full refund; later ones get half. Green cards carry concrete examples, as the source asks (names, exact dates and amounts; docs/bdd/examples.md) [AP]: Priya cancels a £80 booking two days ahead and is refunded £80; Sam cancels a £80 booking six hours ahead and is refunded £40. One red card: what happens to bookings paid with a gift voucher? Nobody can answer it in the session. The source's map keeps that question visible rather than settled in the room (docs/bdd/example-mapping.md, "How it works") [AP]; the builder's harness carries it as an open item the agent may not decide (a harness rule, not the source's).

The examples are formulated as declarative scenarios, with *Priya cancels her booking two days before it starts* rather than a walk through the cancel button, because:

> "The behaviour does not have to change just because the implementation does." (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Describe behaviour") [V]

The operations lead reads and agrees the feature file. The agent then automates one example at a time. The run record shows each scenario failing before the refund logic exists, then passing, which is the source's automation step (docs/bdd/index.md, "Automation: What it _actually does_") [AP]. Partway through, the agent proposes changing Sam's expected refund from £40 to £20 to match what its code returns. The reviewer reads this as a change to the agreed behaviour, not a test fix: the feature file is the specification the client agreed, and the source holds that the documentation reflects the team's shared understanding of the problem domain (docs/bdd/index.md, "Three practices") [AP]. The change goes back to the operations lead, who confirms £40; the agent fixes the code instead.

At review the reviewer checks two things the scenarios hide. First, the `Then` step definitions: one queried the refunds table, which the source says to resist, verifying only "an outcome that is observable for the user (or external system)" (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Then") [V]; the agent rewrites it to check the refund confirmation the customer receives. Second, the run record: six scenarios written, six executed. The warranty pack cites the scenarios, the failing-then-passing runs, the operations lead's agreement, and the open gift-voucher question, which keeps voucher-paid bookings outside the warranty until it is answered. It does not cite "the Cucumber suite is green" as proof on its own, because:

> "Just because you're using Cucumber, doesn't mean you're doing BDD." (docs/bdd/myths.md, "Myth: Using Cucumber means you're doing BDD") [V]

## Anti-patterns This Reference Helps Avoid

- **Prose acceptance criteria.** *Signal:* "works well", "handles errors" with no examples. *Why it fails:* nothing a machine can run, and nothing the client agreed in concrete terms; the source's means is concrete examples (docs/bdd/index.md, "What is BDD?") [AP]. *Instead:* rules with concrete examples under each, agreed before the build.
- **The agent as sole author of the spec.** *Signal:* the agent writes the scenarios from the story and nobody on the business side reads them. *Why it fails:* the source calls discovery left to one individual "not BDD" (docs/bdd/myths.md) [V]; the agent stands in that individual's place here (this distillation's inference). *Instead:* the product owner agrees the scenarios; a pair may write them only under that review (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Writing Gherkin") [AP].
- **Tests written after the code and called the spec.** *Signal:* scenarios appear in the same commit as the implementation, with no failing run. *Why it fails:* automating after the code is test automation, "but it's not BDD" (docs/bdd/myths.md) [V]; the scenario describes what was built, not what was agreed. *Instead:* scenarios agreed and seen failing before the implementation.
- **Moving the spec to fit the code.** *Signal:* a feature file's expected outcome changes in a diff that also changes the code. *Why it fails:* the scenario is the team's agreed understanding, and a behaviour-level scenario need not change when the implementation does (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md) [AR]. *Instead:* treat feature-file edits as spec changes that go back to whoever agreed them (the routing is a harness rule).
- **Procedural scenarios.** *Signal:* steps click buttons and fill fields. *Why it fails:* tied to the current UI, they need more work to maintain and hide the intended behaviour (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Consider a more declarative style") [AP]. *Instead:* declarative steps; mechanics in step definitions.
- **Assertions inside the system.** *Signal:* `Then` steps read the database. *Why it fails:* the source asks for outcomes observable to the user or an external system (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Then") [AP]. *Instead:* assert on the report, screen or message.
- **The tool as the proof.** *Signal:* "we use Cucumber, so the behaviour is specified". *Why it fails:* using Cucumber does not mean the examples were discovered or agreed (docs/bdd/myths.md) [AP]. *Instead:* record who discovered and agreed the scenarios alongside the run.
- **Scenarios that never ran.** *Signal:* the run is green but reports fewer scenarios than exist. *Why it fails:* a stray colon after a keyword makes Cucumber ignore tests (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Reference") [V]. *Instead:* gate on scenarios executed against scenarios written.

## Integration with Other References

| Reference | Relationship |
|---|---|
| `microsoft-code-with-engineering-playbook` | Close agreement on the method. The playbook's test planning builds test cases from a story's acceptance criteria at design time, clarifies ambiguities with the product owner, and writes cases in Given-When-Then form (docs/automated-testing/test-planning.md, "Building test cases for a user story") [AP]; this source supplies the discovery practice and the Gherkin rules behind that form. They differ on how much gets automated: the playbook lets some cases start manual and automates where possible, focusing on hot paths and critical areas, while this source implements every documented example starting from an automated test. Both warn against tests tied to the implementation: the playbook at the unit level (mocks and call verification), this source at the acceptance level (procedural steps, database checks) |
| `uk-duck-book-qa-of-code` | The Duck Book calls test-driven development best practice, writing the test first because the desired outcome is known in advance, and names behaviour-driven and acceptance-test-driven development as extensions focused on user needs (book/testing_code.md, "Write tests before writing logic") [AP]. This source is that extension in full, and adds what the Duck Book leaves out: how the desired outcome gets agreed with the people who know the domain |
| `egashira-testsuitebench-2026` | Complementary at two points. TestSuiteBench found developer documentation too underspecified to generate strong tests from, and test strength fell sharply on it (§2.1; Table 5) [AE]; this source's concrete, agreed examples are one way to write behaviour down in testable detail, though the source measures nothing. And TestSuiteBench found agent tests that check only the shape of the output (App. A.6) [AE]; a declarative scenario hides exact values in its step definitions, so a reviewer who reads only the feature file cannot see whether the assertion pins content (this distillation's inference). Read the two together: this source for what the specification should say, TestSuiteBench for whether the tests would catch a wrong build |
| `jimenez-swe-bench` | SWE-bench requires each task to have at least one test that changes from fail to pass when the reference fix is applied, and evaluates a patch by applying the tests from the human pull request that resolved the issue (§2.1, Stage III; App. A.4) [AP]. This source's automation step also starts from a test that fails before the behaviour exists. Together they support one ledger rule: a new behaviour's evidence is a test seen failing, then passing, that the agent did not get to redefine |
| `why-language-models-hallucinate-kalai` | Kalai et al. argue that binary grading rewards a model for guessing over abstaining (§1.2) [AP]. Example Mapping's red cards are a place to record "we don't know yet" instead of an answer. Pairing them is this distillation's inference: an agent asked to fill a gap the spec leaves open is in the guessing regime Kalai et al. describe, and a red card keeps the gap visible |
| `uk-aqua-book-2025` | The Aqua Book's engagement and scoping stage has commissioner and analyst develop a shared understanding of the problem and context, the basis for designing the analysis (Ch 6, "Engagement and scoping") [AP]. This source's discovery workshop is the software-team version: shared understanding with the business, built from examples, before formulation |

## Citation and Source-Integrity Notes

**Borrowed-through gaps.** The source cites prior work it does not reproduce: an epigraph on deciding what to build, a practitioner's ordering of the three practices quoted to answer the first myth, earlier writers credited with the origins of BDD and of the Given/When/Then template, and linked pages on Example Mapping, other workshop models and lower-level test examples [BT]. None of these is held in this corpus, and this distillation relies only on what the Cucumber pages themselves say.

**Named limits of the source.** The source is product documentation: no studies, no measurements, no comparison of BDD with other ways of working. Workshop size and length, steps per example and `Background` length are rules of thumb [AP]. It says nothing about coding agents; every application to an agent harness here is this distillation's inference. It is an operator-approved subset: pages it links to (step definitions, tags and hooks, the anti-patterns guide) are not covered, so nothing here describes how Cucumber reports undefined or pending steps. Its rule against checking the database is stated for `Then` steps in acceptance scenarios; the source points to lower-level examples for internal components and does not extend the rule to them.

**Evidence-marker continuity.** Recommendations carry `[AP]`, and the documentation's arguments (the order of the practices, the case for declarative style, the need for all roles in discovery) carry `[AR]`, as in the deep reference. Verbatim passages are copied from the deep reference's audited `[V]` quotations; none was re-extracted from the tape. Integration rows cite the sibling deep references' own sections and markers.

## Runtime triggers this source addresses

| Trigger | Content from this source that addresses it | Teach-in-the-moment script |
|---|---|---|
| The story's acceptance criteria are prose ("works well", "handles errors") with no runnable check (Phase 1) | Concrete examples guide the work from concept to implementation, formulated in a medium people and machines both read and automated before the code (docs/bdd/index.md) [AP] | Prose can't fail a test. Put a concrete example under each criterion, with names and amounts, and agree them before the agent starts. |
| Nobody can say who will use the change or what they will do with it (Phase 1) | Discovery with the product owner, a developer and a tester; the feature header's `In order to`, `As a` and `I want` lines "cover Why, Who, and What" (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md) [V] | If you can't write the Why, Who and What lines, you aren't ready to build. Spend half an hour with the person who knows the users first. |
| The spec is long and the change is large (Phase 1) | A story needing more than about 25-30 minutes of discovery is probably too large; a scenario that cannot be said in one sentence covers too much; 3-5 steps per example (docs/bdd/discovery-workshop.md; docs/bdd/who-does-what.md; docs/gherkin/reference.md) [AP] | If the examples won't fit a short conversation, the change is too big to warrant as one. Split it and defer what can wait. |
| The builder says "the agent will figure out the details" (Phase 1) | Discovery may "reveal gaps in our understanding, where we need more information before we know what to do" (docs/bdd/index.md) [V]; unanswerable questions go on red cards (docs/bdd/example-mapping.md) [AP] | The details the agent would figure out are the red cards. Write them down as open, and don't let the agent close them silently. |
| The agent is asked to "build X like Y" with no statement of what must not change (Phase 1) | Automated examples show what the system currently does and let the team change it without unintentionally breaking anything; behaviour-level scenarios need not change when the implementation does (docs/bdd/index.md; docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md) [AP] | What must not change is whatever the existing scenarios say. If there are none for this area, write them before the rework. (Applying this to agent rework is this distillation's inference.) |
| The agent proposes changing a test so the build goes green (Phase 3) | The scenario holds the agreed behaviour and the step definition holds the implementation; "The intent of the scenario remains the same, even if the implementation changes later." (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md) [V] | Ask which file it wants to change. A feature-file change changes the agreed behaviour and goes back to whoever agreed it; locking it is a harness rule. |
| The tests were written by the same agent session after the code (Phase 3) | Automating after the code is "a perfectly reasonable way to do test automation, but it's not BDD" (docs/bdd/myths.md) [V]; the source automates each example before the code, as a test that fails first (docs/bdd/index.md) [AP] | These tests describe what was built, not what was agreed. Count them as asserted until scenarios agreed beforehand have been seen failing and then passing. |
| A test checks the agent's output text rather than the system's state (Phase 3) | `Then` steps assert the actual outcome against the expected one, on output observable to the user or an external system (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Then") [AP] | Check what the system shows its user, not what the agent says it did. (The source also warns against checking the database; it names observable output as the target.) |
| The suite passes, but nobody knows whether it would catch a wrong implementation (Phase 3) | Each automated example starts as a test that fails because the behaviour isn't there yet (docs/bdd/index.md) [AP] | Partial answer: a scenario seen failing before the code at least can fail. It does not measure strength; that needs seeded faults (see `egashira-testsuitebench-2026`). |
| The agent runs for an hour unattended and reports success (Phase 4) | Automation takes one example at a time, failing then passing, in small rapid iterations (docs/bdd/index.md, "Three practices") [AP] | Ask for the run record per scenario: failed, implemented, passed. One green run at the end is a claim, not that sequence. |
| "It worked first time", or a flaky check passed on retry (Phase 5) | The automation step expects the new test to fail first, because the behaviour is not implemented yet (docs/bdd/index.md) [AP] | A new scenario that passed before its code existed isn't testing the new behaviour. Find out what it checks. (The source does not address flaky checks.) |
| The builder approves because reading the diff is too slow (Phase 6) | Gherkin is "a medium that can be read by both humans and computers" [V]; the product owner actively reviews the scenarios a pair writes (docs/bdd/index.md; docs/bdd/who-does-what.md) [AP] | Read the scenarios and the run record instead of the diff, and have the client's side confirm the scenarios say what they need. |
| The same session that wrote the code reviews it (Phase 6) | Discovery left to a single individual is "not BDD" [V]; each role sees the product from a different perspective, so all should discover examples together (docs/bdd/myths.md; docs/bdd/who-does-what.md) [AR] | At least the scenarios need eyes from another role: the client's side for scope, a tester's eye for how it breaks. (Extending this from discovery to review is this distillation's inference.) |
| Nobody could explain how this part works if the agent were unavailable (Phase 7) | "The code reflects the documentation, and the documentation reflects the team's shared understanding of the problem domain." (docs/bdd/index.md) [V] | If the feature files don't explain this area in the client's language, nobody holds its theory. Write the scenarios before signing. |

## Trigger extensions surfaced by this source

| Phase | Trigger (what the practitioner notices) | Response (grounded in this source) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Discovery for one story runs well past half an hour | Split the story or set it aside for research: needing more time suggests it is too large or missing specifics (docs/bdd/discovery-workshop.md) [AP] |
| 1 | Questions come up that nobody present can answer | Record each as an open question (a red card) instead of letting the agent answer it; carry open questions on the warranty pack (docs/bdd/example-mapping.md) [AP]. Barring the agent from closing them is a harness rule |
| 1 | Scenario steps name buttons, fields or URLs | Ask "Will this wording need to change if the implementation does?" and rewrite declaratively (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md) [V] |
| 1 / 6 | The agent wrote the scenarios and nobody on the business side has read them | Route them to the product owner for review before they are locked: discovery by one party is "not BDD" (docs/bdd/myths.md) [V] |
| 3 | A diff edits a feature file's expected outcome alongside the code | Treat the feature-file edit as a change to the agreed behaviour and route it to whoever agreed it; behaviour need not change because the implementation does (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md) [V] |
| 3 | A `Then` step definition queries the database | Rewrite it to assert on output observable to the user or an external system (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Then") [V] |
| 3 / 6 | Declarative scenarios read well, but nobody has read the step definitions behind the `Then` steps | Read the step definitions: in the declarative style, exact values live there (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md) [AP]. That the assertion's strength therefore lives there is this distillation's inference |
| 4 | The agent wrote step definitions for steps no scenario uses | Remove them: "Don't write step definitions for steps that are not present in one of your scenarios." (docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx) [V] |
| 4 | The agent added near-duplicate steps | Collapse them into one parameterised step backed by helper methods (docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx, "Avoid duplication") [AP] |
| 5 | The run reports fewer scenarios than the feature files contain | Block until they match: a colon after a keyword that should not have one means "your test(s) will be ignored" (docs/gherkin/reference.md) [V]. Counting scenarios at the gate is a harness rule |
| 5 | A new scenario passed on its first run, before its implementation | Find out what it checks; the source's automation step expects a failing test first (docs/bdd/index.md) [AP] |
| 7 | The pack cites "the Cucumber suite is green" as proof the behaviour is what the client wanted | Ask who discovered and agreed the scenarios: "Just because you're using Cucumber, doesn't mean you're doing BDD." (docs/bdd/myths.md) [V] |
| 8 | The documentation says the system does one thing and the system does another | Keep the description of the behaviour executable, so the documentation is automatically checked against what the system does (docs/bdd/index.md, "What is BDD?") [AP] |
